migrations.name: The first farmers reach Europe
migrations.summary: Farming began in the Fertile Crescent, and from about 7000 BC farmers from Anatolia carried wheat, barley, sheep, goats and pottery into Europe, family by family and generation by generation. Ancient DNA shows they were newcomers, not locals copying a new idea: they mixed with the hunter-gatherers they met but largely replaced them. By 4000 BC fields reached from Greece to Britain and Scandinavia.
migrations.numbers: A few kilometres a generation, for three thousand years

steps.label: c. 7000 BC
steps.title: Out of Anatolia
steps.text: Villages like Catalhoyuk in central Anatolia had farmed for two thousand years. Their people spread west to the Aegean coast and crossed into Greece, where the first farming villages of Europe appear in Thessaly about 6500 BC.

sites.name: Catalhoyuk
sites.text: A town of mud-brick houses entered through the roof, home to thousands of early farmers.

sites.name: Sesklo
sites.text: One of the first farming villages in Europe.

steps.label: c. 6200 to 5000 BC
steps.title: Up the Danube
steps.text: One stream followed the rivers north. Farmers of the Starcevo culture filled the Balkans; the Linear Pottery people then raced across the loess soils of central Europe in a few centuries, building longhouses from Hungary to the Paris basin.

sites.name: Linear Pottery longhouses
sites.text: Timber longhouses up to 40 metres long, the first villages of central Europe.

steps.label: c. 6000 to 5400 BC
steps.title: Along the Mediterranean shore
steps.text: Another stream went by boat, hopping along the coasts of the Adriatic, Italy, southern France and Spain. Archaeologists follow them by their pots, decorated with the edge of a cockle shell.

steps.label: c. 4500 to 3800 BC
steps.title: To Britain and the north
steps.text: After a long pause on the edge of the North European Plain, farming crossed the Channel to Britain and Ireland about 4000 BC, and reached southern Scandinavia. Within a few centuries the first great stone monuments rose along the Atlantic.

sites.name: Carnac
sites.text: Thousands of standing stones raised by the first farmers of Brittany.

migrations.name: The steppe herders (Indo-Europeans)
migrations.summary: From about 3300 BC herders of the Pontic steppe, the Yamnaya, took to wagons and horses and spread east and west. Their descendants carried Indo-European languages from Ireland to India: the ancestors of English, Latin, Greek, Russian, Persian and Sanskrit. Ancient DNA shows a huge movement of people into Europe about 2800 BC, and into South Asia after 2000 BC, mixing with the farmers already there.
migrations.numbers: Ancestors of nearly half the world's languages

steps.label: c. 3300 to 3000 BC
steps.title: The Yamnaya
steps.text: On the grasslands north of the Black Sea, herders with ox-drawn wagons and horses could live on the move. Their kurgans, burial mounds, run from the Danube to the Urals, and one branch went 2,000 km east to the Altai mountains.

sites.name: Yamnaya kurgans
sites.text: Burial mounds of the steppe herders, with wagons buried beside the dead.

steps.label: c. 3000 to 2400 BC
steps.title: Into Europe
steps.text: Steppe people pushed up the Danube and across the plains north of the Carpathians. In central Europe they became the Corded Ware culture; within a few centuries most of the ancestry of northern Europeans came from the steppe. The Bell Beaker people carried it on to Britain.

sites.name: Amesbury Archer
sites.text: A man born in the Alps and buried near Stonehenge with the richest Beaker grave in Britain.

steps.label: c. 2300 to 1900 BC
steps.title: Anatolia and the Tarim
steps.text: Other speakers reached Anatolia, where the Hittites would write the oldest Indo-European texts, and the ancestors of the Tocharians settled the oases of the Tarim basin, where their mummies, in woollen tartans, still lie in the desert.

sites.name: Hattusa
sites.text: Capital of the Hittites, whose tablets are the oldest written Indo-European.

sites.name: Xiaohe cemetery
sites.text: Mummies of the Tarim basin, buried under boat-shaped coffins.

steps.label: c. 2100 to 1700 BC
steps.title: The chariot people of the Urals
steps.text: East of the Urals the Sintashta people built fortified towns and the first spoked-wheel chariots. Their successors, the Andronovo herders, spread across the steppe of Kazakhstan to the edge of the Bactrian oases.

sites.name: Sintashta
sites.text: Fortified town where the oldest spoked-wheel chariots were buried.

steps.label: c. 1700 to 1400 BC
steps.title: Into Iran and India
steps.text: Indo-Iranian speakers moved south through Bactria. One branch became the Iranian peoples; another, the Indo-Aryans, crossed the Hindu Kush into the Punjab, where the Rigveda was composed in Sanskrit. Indo-Aryan names even appear among the kings of Mitanni in Syria.

migrations.name: The Austronesian voyagers
migrations.summary: From Taiwan about 3000 BC, farmers and sailors in outrigger canoes spread through the islands of Southeast Asia and out into the Pacific and the Indian Ocean. Their languages, over 1,200 of them, run from Madagascar to Easter Island, more than halfway around the world: Malay, Tagalog, Javanese, Malagasy, Maori and Hawaiian are all Austronesian.
migrations.numbers: Over 1,200 languages, from Madagascar to Rapa Nui

steps.label: c. 3000 to 2000 BC
steps.title: Out of Taiwan
steps.text: Rice farmers of Taiwan crossed the Luzon Strait to the Philippines about 2200 BC, then island-hopped south with pigs, dogs and pottery, sailing outrigger canoes that could carry families and seed.

sites.name: Batanes Islands
sites.text: Stepping stones between Taiwan and Luzon, where the oldest Philippine red-slipped pottery is found.

steps.label: c. 2000 to 1500 BC
steps.title: Through the islands
steps.text: They spread through Borneo, Sulawesi, Java and the Moluccas, meeting the older peoples of the region and mixing with them. At the edge of New Guinea they turned east, out into the open Pacific.

steps.label: c. 1500 to 800 BC
steps.title: The Lapita people
steps.text: In the Bismarck Archipelago the voyagers became the Lapita people, known for their stamped pottery. In a few centuries they crossed thousands of kilometres of open sea to Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, islands no human had ever seen.

sites.name: Lapita
sites.text: The site on New Caledonia that gave its name to the first Pacific voyagers.

steps.label: c. AD 200 to 600
steps.title: Across the Indian Ocean
steps.text: Westward, sailors from Borneo crossed the whole Indian Ocean. They settled Madagascar, where Malagasy, a language close to one spoken in southern Borneo, is still spoken, along with bananas and outrigger canoes on the African coast.

sites.name: Madagascar
sites.text: Settled by Austronesians from Borneo, later joined by Bantu-speaking Africans.

migrations.name: The Bantu expansion
migrations.summary: From the grasslands of Cameroon, farmers speaking Bantu languages spread over most of Africa south of the equator in about two thousand years, through the rainforest and around it, learning to work iron on the way. It was one of the largest movements of people in history: today some 350 million people speak over 500 Bantu languages, from Swahili and Kikongo to Zulu and Xhosa.

steps.label: c. 2000 to 1000 BC
steps.title: From the Cameroon grasslands
steps.text: The first Bantu farmers grew yams and oil palms and fished the rivers. They moved south into the equatorial forest, along the rivers and the coast, settling clearings for a few generations and then moving on.

sites.name: Cameroon grasslands
sites.text: The homeland of the Bantu languages, near today's border of Nigeria and Cameroon.

steps.label: c. 1500 to 500 BC
steps.title: Around the forest to the Great Lakes
steps.text: An eastern stream skirted the northern edge of the rainforest and reached the Great Lakes, where people learned to smelt iron and herd cattle. Urewe pottery and iron furnaces mark them around Lake Victoria by 500 BC.

sites.name: Urewe
sites.text: Early ironworking farmers on the shores of Lake Victoria.

steps.label: c. 500 BC to AD 100
steps.title: West to Angola
steps.text: The western stream crossed the lower Congo and moved down into the savannas of Angola, reaching the edge of the Namib desert, home of the Khoisan herders and foragers.

steps.label: c. 200 BC to AD 500
steps.title: Iron down the east
steps.text: From the Great Lakes, iron-using farmers spread fast down the eastern side of the continent: through Tanzania, Malawi and Zambia to Zimbabwe, and along the coast to Mozambique, reaching today's KwaZulu-Natal by about AD 400.

sites.name: Great Zimbabwe
sites.text: Later, about 1100, Bantu-speaking Shona built the stone city of Great Zimbabwe here.

migrations.name: The Sea Peoples
migrations.summary: About 1200 BC, as the palace kingdoms of the Bronze Age collapsed, bands of warriors and whole families, the "Sea Peoples" of Egyptian records, moved by land and sea through Anatolia, Cyprus and the Levant. Ugarit and other cities burned. Ramesses III fought them off at the mouth of the Nile, and one group, the Peleset, settled the coast of Canaan as the Philistines.

steps.label: c. 1210 to 1185 BC
steps.title: Raiders from the Aegean
steps.text: Who they were is still argued: Mycenaean Greeks, Sardinians, Sicilians, Anatolians, driven perhaps by drought, famine and the fall of their own kingdoms. Letters from Ugarit beg for help against enemy ships just before the city burned.

sites.name: Ugarit
sites.text: A rich port of Syria, destroyed and never rebuilt.

steps.label: c. 1185 to 1150 BC
steps.title: To the gates of Egypt
steps.text: They came down the coast with ox carts carrying women and children. In about 1177 BC Ramesses III met them on land and in the Nile delta, and carved the victory on his temple at Medinet Habu. The defeated Peleset settled Gaza, Ashkelon and Ashdod.

sites.name: Battle of the Delta
sites.text: Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples at the Nile mouths.

sites.name: Philistia
sites.text: Gaza, Ashkelon and Ashdod: the Philistines' new home.

migrations.name: Phoenician colonists
migrations.summary: The merchant cities of Phoenicia, Tyre above all, sent colonists across the whole Mediterranean to the Atlantic, founding trading posts that grew into cities: Kition on Cyprus, Utica, Carthage, Motya in Sicily, Nora in Sardinia and Gadir, today's Cadiz. They carried the alphabet with them.

steps.label: c. 1100 to 800 BC
steps.title: West from Tyre
steps.text: Hemmed in between the mountains and the sea, the Phoenicians looked west for silver, tin and trade. Tradition puts the founding of Gadir beyond the Pillars of Hercules as early as 1100 BC; the oldest remains there date from about 800 BC.

sites.name: Tyre
sites.text: Island city of Phoenicia, famous for its purple dye.

sites.name: Gadir
sites.text: Cadiz, the Phoenicians' gateway to the Atlantic.

steps.label: c. 814 to 650 BC
steps.title: Carthage, the new city
steps.text: In legend, Princess Elissa (Dido) fled Tyre and founded Qart-hadasht, the "new city", in 814 BC. Carthage became the greatest Phoenician city of all, founding its own colonies in Sicily, Sardinia, Ibiza and Spain.

sites.name: Carthage
sites.text: Founded by colonists from Tyre; for six centuries the rival of Greeks and Romans.

migrations.name: Rice farmers reach Japan (Yayoi)
migrations.summary: From about 900 BC, rice farmers from the Korean peninsula crossed to northern Kyushu, bringing wet-rice paddies, bronze and then iron. The Yayoi culture they began spread up the Japanese islands over the next thousand years, mixing with the Jomon people, foragers who had lived there for over ten thousand years. Most Japanese today descend from both.

steps.label: c. 900 to 400 BC
steps.title: Across the Tsushima Strait
steps.text: The first paddy fields of Japan, at Itazuke near Fukuoka, look just like those of southern Korea. Newcomers and Jomon locals farmed side by side.

sites.name: Itazuke
sites.text: Some of the oldest rice paddies in Japan.

steps.label: c. 400 to 100 BC
steps.title: East through Honshu
steps.text: Rice farming spread along the Inland Sea to the Kinai plain and then north and east, though in cold northern Honshu and Hokkaido people kept the Jomon way of life much longer.

sites.name: Yoshinogari
sites.text: A great moated Yayoi town in Kyushu.

migrations.name: Greek colonists
migrations.summary: Between about 775 and 550 BC Greek cities short of farmland sent out bands of colonists, chosen by lot and blessed by the oracle at Delphi. They founded hundreds of cities from Spain to the Crimea: Syracuse, Naples, Marseille, Byzantium and Cyrene among them. Southern Italy became Magna Graecia, "Great Greece", and the Mediterranean, in Plato's words, a pond with Greeks around it like frogs.

steps.label: c. 775 to 700 BC
steps.title: To Sicily and Italy
steps.text: Euboeans settled Pithekoussai on Ischia and then Cumae, near Naples. Corinth founded Syracuse in 733 BC, Sparta founded Taras (Taranto) in 706. The fertile plains of the west filled with Greek cities.

sites.name: Syracuse
sites.text: Founded by Corinth; it became the greatest city of the Greek west.

sites.name: Pithekoussai
sites.text: On Ischia: the oldest Greek settlement in the west.

steps.label: c. 680 to 600 BC
steps.title: To the Black Sea
steps.text: Miletus alone was said to have founded ninety colonies. Greeks settled the straits, where Megara founded Byzantium about 667 BC, and then the shores of the Black Sea, trading wine and olive oil for the grain of the steppe.

sites.name: Byzantium
sites.text: Founded by Megara on the Bosporus; later Constantinople and Istanbul.

sites.name: Olbia
sites.text: Milesian colony at the mouth of the Bug, trading with the Scythians.

steps.label: c. 630 to 550 BC
steps.title: To Africa and Gaul
steps.text: Settlers from the island of Thera founded Cyrene in Libya about 630 BC, after the oracle told them to. Greeks from Phocaea in Asia Minor sailed to the far west and founded Massalia, Marseille, about 600 BC.

sites.name: Massalia
sites.text: Marseille, founded by Greeks from Phocaea.

sites.name: Cyrene
sites.text: The great Greek city of Libya.

migrations.name: The Babylonian exile
migrations.summary: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took Jerusalem in 597 BC and carried its king and thousands of its people into exile; in 587 BC he destroyed the city and the Temple and deported more. By the rivers of Babylon the exiles kept their faith and began to gather their scriptures. When Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC he let them go home, and the Second Temple was finished in 515 BC.

steps.label: 597 to 582 BC
steps.title: By the rivers of Babylon
steps.text: The deportees walked some 1,300 km around the desert, by the Euphrates, to Babylonia, where they were settled in villages like Al-Yahudu, "Judah town", whose clay tablets have been found.

sites.name: Jerusalem
sites.text: Nebuchadnezzar destroys the city and Solomon's Temple.

sites.name: Babylon
sites.text: Where the exiles lived for two generations.

steps.label: 538 to 515 BC
steps.title: The return
steps.text: Cyrus's decree allowed the exiles to return and rebuild. Many went home under Zerubbabel; many stayed, and Babylonia remained a great centre of Jewish life for fifteen hundred years.

sites.name: Second Temple
sites.text: The rebuilt Temple, finished in 515 BC.

migrations.name: The Arawaks settle the Caribbean
migrations.summary: From the Orinoco delta, farming peoples speaking Arawakan languages paddled great dugout canoes up the chain of the Lesser Antilles, reaching Puerto Rico about 400 BC. Their descendants, the Taino, spread over Hispaniola, Cuba, Jamaica and the Bahamas, where Columbus met them in 1492. Later the Kalinago (Island Caribs) followed the same path.

steps.label: c. 500 BC to AD 600
steps.title: Up the island chain
steps.text: The Saladoid people, named after their white-on-red pottery, came out of the Orinoco and settled island after island within sight of the next, until they reached Puerto Rico and Hispaniola.

sites.name: Orinoco delta
sites.text: Homeland of the Arawakan farmers who settled the islands.

steps.label: c. 600 to 1450
steps.title: The Taino world
steps.text: From Hispaniola the Taino settled Cuba, Jamaica and the Bahamas, growing cassava, playing a ball game in stone courts. Kalinago warriors moved up the Lesser Antilles from about 1200, taking the islands from the Arawaks.

sites.name: Guanahani
sites.text: Taino island in the Bahamas where Columbus landed in 1492.

migrations.name: The Celts on the move
migrations.summary: From their heartland north of the Alps, Celtic peoples moved south and east in the fourth and third centuries BC. Gauls took the Po valley and sacked Rome in 390 BC; later bands crossed the Balkans, plundered Delphi in 279 BC, and three tribes went on into Asia Minor, where they settled as the Galatians, to whom St Paul later wrote.

steps.label: c. 450 to 390 BC
steps.title: Over the Alps into Italy
steps.text: Senones, Boii, Insubres and other tribes crossed the Alps and drove the Etruscans out of the Po valley, which the Romans came to call Cisalpine Gaul. In 390 BC the Senones beat a Roman army on the Allia and sacked Rome.

sites.name: La Tene
sites.text: On Lake Neuchatel; its name is given to Celtic art and culture of the time.

sites.name: Sack of Rome
sites.text: Brennus and the Senones take Rome: "Vae victis", woe to the conquered.

steps.label: c. 335 to 278 BC
steps.title: Down the Danube to Delphi
steps.text: Celtic bands moved down the Danube into the Balkans. In 279 BC Brennus led a great army through Macedonia to Delphi, where the Greeks beat them back in a storm. Some settled on the Danube, where Belgrade began as their Singidunum.

sites.name: Delphi
sites.text: The Gauls' attack on the sanctuary fails in snow and earthquake.

steps.label: c. 278 to 270 BC
steps.title: The Galatians in Asia
steps.text: Some 20,000 Celts, with their families, crossed the Hellespont in 278 BC, hired by the king of Bithynia. After years of raiding they were settled in central Anatolia around Ancyra, today's Ankara, which became Galatia.

sites.name: Ancyra
sites.text: Today's Ankara, chief town of the Galatians.

migrations.name: The Yuezhi go west
migrations.summary: The Yuezhi, horse nomads of the Gansu corridor, were driven out by the Xiongnu about 176 BC; their king's skull, the story goes, became a Xiongnu drinking cup. They rode 3,000 km west, through the Ili valley to Bactria, where they conquered the last Greek kingdom of the east. One of their clans founded the Kushan Empire, which joined the trade of Rome, Persia, India and China.

steps.label: 176 to 130 BC
steps.title: Driven from Gansu
steps.text: Beaten by the Xiongnu, the Yuezhi fled to the Ili valley; pushed on again by the Wusun, they moved to the Oxus and crossed it into Bactria about 130 BC.

sites.name: Hexi Corridor
sites.text: The Yuezhi homeland between the Qilian mountains and the desert.

steps.label: 128 BC to AD 30
steps.title: Masters of Bactria
steps.text: The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian found them in 128 BC, settled and rich, and uninterested in revenge on the Xiongnu. In the first century AD their Kushan clan united the rest and pushed south over the Hindu Kush.

sites.name: Zhang Qian
sites.text: China's envoy reaches the Yuezhi; his journey opens the Silk Road.

migrations.name: The Cimbri and Teutons
migrations.summary: About 120 BC the Cimbri and Teutons left Jutland, perhaps after floods, and wandered through Europe for twenty years with their wagons, families and herds, looking for land. They crushed Roman armies, worst at Arausio in 105 BC, before Gaius Marius destroyed them at Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae. Rome never forgot the terror from the north.

steps.label: 120 to 105 BC
steps.title: Out of Jutland
steps.text: The tribes went south to the Danube, beat a Roman army at Noreia in 113 BC, turned west into Gaul, and in 105 BC destroyed two Roman armies at Arausio (Orange): tens of thousands of Romans died, one of Rome's worst defeats.

sites.name: Arausio
sites.text: Two Roman armies destroyed by the Cimbri.

steps.label: 104 to 101 BC
steps.title: Marius stops them
steps.text: After a raid into Spain the tribes split to invade Italy. Marius, with a newly reformed army, destroyed the Teutons at Aquae Sextiae in 102 BC and the Cimbri at Vercellae in 101 BC.

sites.name: Aquae Sextiae
sites.text: Marius destroys the Teutons near Aix-en-Provence.

sites.name: Vercellae
sites.text: The Cimbri are annihilated in the Po valley.

migrations.name: The Goths go south to the Black Sea
migrations.summary: Roman writers and the Goths' own legends say they came from Scandza, Scandinavia, to the lower Vistula. Archaeology follows the Wielbark culture of the Vistula south-east to the Black Sea in the second and third centuries, where the Goths built a great realm on the steppe and the forest edge, and from there raided deep into the Roman Empire.

steps.label: c. 150 to 230
steps.title: From the Vistula to the Black Sea
steps.text: Families with wagons and cattle moved up the Vistula and over to the Dnieper and the Dniester, settling among the peoples of the steppe edge. Their Chernyakhov culture of villages spread from Romania to Ukraine.

sites.name: Wielbark
sites.text: The Gothic homeland on the lower Vistula, in archaeology.

steps.label: 238 to 270
steps.title: Raiders of the empire
steps.text: Goths crossed the Danube and killed Emperor Decius at Abritus in 251, the first emperor to die fighting a foreign foe. By ship they raided the Aegean and sacked Athens in 267, until Claudius II beat them at Naissus in 268.

sites.name: Abritus
sites.text: Emperor Decius dies in battle against the Goths.

sites.name: Naissus
sites.text: Claudius II beats the Goths: they called him Gothicus.

migrations.name: The Chinese flights to the south
migrations.summary: Twice the people of the north China plain fled south in their millions. When the Xiongnu sacked Luoyang in 311, nobles, scholars and farmers crossed the Yangtze to found a new court at Jiankang (Nanjing): the "clothes and caps went south". In 1127 the Jurchen took Kaifeng and the Song court fled again, to Hangzhou. Each time the south grew richer, until it became China's heart.

steps.label: 307 to 330
steps.title: The clothes and caps go south
steps.text: After the Disaster of Yongjia in 311, when Luoyang was sacked and the emperor taken, perhaps a million northerners went south over a generation. The Eastern Jin dynasty ruled from Jiankang.

sites.name: Luoyang
sites.text: Sacked by the Xiongnu in 311; tens of thousands killed.

sites.name: Jiankang
sites.text: Nanjing, capital of the Eastern Jin and the southern dynasties.

steps.label: 1127 to 1140
steps.title: The Song cross the Yangtze
steps.text: When the Jurchen Jin took Kaifeng in 1127 and carried off two emperors, a prince of the Song fled south. Millions followed; the Southern Song made Hangzhou, then the largest city on earth, their capital.

sites.name: Kaifeng
sites.text: The Song capital falls to the Jurchen.

sites.name: Hangzhou
sites.text: The Southern Song capital, Marco Polo's "Quinsai".

migrations.name: The Huns
migrations.summary: About 370 a people of mounted archers from the steppe of Central Asia crossed the Volga, conquered the Alans and smashed the Gothic kingdoms north of the Black Sea, setting off the great migrations into the Roman Empire. Under Attila, from 434, the Huns ruled from the Rhine to the Caspian. After his death in 453 their empire broke apart within a year.

steps.label: c. 350 to 376
steps.title: Out of the steppe
steps.text: Where the Huns came from is still argued; many think they had among their ancestors the Xiongnu who once fought China. They fell on the Alans by the Don and then on the Greuthungi Goths, whose old king Ermanaric took his own life.

steps.label: 400 to 434
steps.title: Masters of the Danube
steps.text: The Huns moved their camp to the Hungarian plain, ruling Goths, Gepids, Alans and others, raiding the Balkans and taking huge payments of gold from Constantinople.

sites.name: Attila's camp
sites.text: A town of timber halls on the Hungarian plain, described by the envoy Priscus.

steps.label: 441 to 452
steps.title: Attila
steps.text: Attila ravaged the Balkans, then in 451 rode west into Gaul with Germanic allies and was stopped by Aetius's Romans and Visigoths on the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he invaded Italy, sacked Aquileia, and turned back after meeting Pope Leo.

sites.name: Catalaunian Plains
sites.text: Aetius, Theodoric of the Visigoths and their allies halt Attila.

sites.name: Aquileia
sites.text: Sacked so thoroughly that refugees fled to the lagoons where Venice would grow.

steps.label: 453 to 469
steps.title: The end of the Huns
steps.text: Attila died on his wedding night in 453. His sons quarrelled, the subject peoples rose and beat them at the Nedao in 454, and the Huns went back east to the steppe, where they vanish from history after 469.

sites.name: Nedao
sites.text: Gepids, Ostrogoths and others break the power of Attila's sons.

migrations.name: The Franks take Gaul
migrations.summary: The Franks were a league of Germanic peoples on the lower Rhine. Rome let the Salian Franks settle in Toxandria in 358 as allies; as Roman power faded they spread south over northern Gaul. Clovis, king from 481, beat the last Roman ruler at Soissons, the Alemanni and the Visigoths, became a Catholic Christian, and made Paris the capital of the kingdom that gave France its name.

steps.label: 358 to 460
steps.title: Over the lower Rhine
steps.text: The Franks moved slowly, farming families more than a marching army, from the Rhine mouths into today's Belgium. Childeric, Clovis's father, ruled from Tournai, where his grave was found full of gold bees.

sites.name: Tournai
sites.text: Childeric's capital and grave.

steps.label: 486 to 511
steps.title: Clovis
steps.text: Clovis took Soissons from Syagrius in 486, was baptised at Reims, beat the Visigoths at Vouille in 507 and drove them into Spain. He made Paris his capital; by his death in 511 the Franks held almost all of Gaul.

sites.name: Soissons
sites.text: Clovis ends the last Roman state in Gaul.

sites.name: Vouille
sites.text: Clovis kills Alaric II and takes Aquitaine from the Visigoths.

migrations.name: The Visigoths
migrations.summary: Fleeing the Huns, tens of thousands of Goths begged to be let into the Roman Empire in 376. Cheated and starved by Roman officials, they rose up, destroyed an emperor's army at Adrianople, and spent forty years on the move inside the empire. Under Alaric they sacked Rome in 410, the first time in 800 years the city fell to a foreign enemy, and in 418 they were given land in Aquitaine, where their kingdom of Toulouse began.
migrations.numbers: About 100,000 people, a fifth of them warriors

steps.label: 376 to 382
steps.title: Across the Danube
steps.text: The Romans ferried the Goths over the Danube but sold them dogs to eat in exchange for their children. The Goths revolted, and on 9 August 378 at Adrianople they killed Emperor Valens and two thirds of his army. In 382 they were settled in the Balkans as allies.

sites.name: Adrianople
sites.text: Emperor Valens and his army are destroyed by the Goths.

steps.label: 395 to 408
steps.title: Alaric
steps.text: Alaric, chosen king, led his people through Greece in 395 to 397 and then into Italy, looking for land and a Roman command. Stilicho beat him back at Pollentia in 402, but when Stilicho was murdered in 408 nothing stood in Alaric's way.

sites.name: Pollentia
sites.text: Stilicho stops Alaric's first invasion of Italy.

steps.label: 408 to 412
steps.title: The sack of Rome
steps.text: After three sieges Alaric's Goths broke into Rome on 24 August 410 and plundered it for three days. The shock ran through the Roman world; Augustine wrote The City of God in answer. Alaric died weeks later in Calabria, buried in a riverbed with his treasure.

sites.name: Rome
sites.text: Sacked by Alaric's Goths on 24 August 410.

sites.name: Cosenza
sites.text: Alaric dies; his men divert the river Busento to bury him.

steps.label: 412 to 418
steps.title: A kingdom in Gaul
steps.text: Under Athaulf, who married the emperor's sister Galla Placidia, the Goths moved into southern Gaul and Spain. In 418 Rome settled them in Aquitaine as allies. Their kingdom of Toulouse later moved to Spain, ruling it from Toledo until 711.

sites.name: Toulouse
sites.text: Capital of the Visigothic kingdom until 507.

migrations.name: Vandals, Alans and Suebi
migrations.summary: On the last day of 406, a host of Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine, perhaps over the frozen river near Mainz, and ravaged Gaul. Three years later they crossed into Spain. The Vandals went on to Africa in 429 and took Carthage in 439, the richest city of the West, and from there sacked Rome in 455, so thoroughly that "vandalism" bears their name.
migrations.numbers: About 80,000 Vandals and Alans crossed to Africa

steps.label: 401 to 406
steps.title: The crossing of the Rhine
steps.text: Driven west by the Huns, the peoples gathered on the middle Rhine. On 31 December 406 they broke through the Frankish allies guarding the frontier and poured into Gaul. The Burgundians followed and settled around Worms.

sites.name: Mainz
sites.text: The Rhine frontier breaks on the last day of 406.

sites.name: Worms
sites.text: The Burgundian kingdom of the Nibelungenlied, destroyed by Aetius's Huns in 436.

steps.label: 407 to 409
steps.title: Through Gaul to Spain
steps.text: For two years the host plundered Gaul: Reims, Trier, Arras, Tours, down to the Pyrenees. In autumn 409 they crossed into Spain and shared it out: the Suebi took Galicia, the Alans Lusitania, the Vandals the south.

sites.name: Braga
sites.text: Capital of the Suebi kingdom in Galicia, which lasted until 585.

steps.label: 429 to 439
steps.title: To Africa
steps.text: In May 429 King Gaiseric ferried his whole people, 80,000 strong, across the Strait of Gibraltar and marched east along the coast. They besieged Hippo, where St Augustine died in 430, and in 439 took Carthage by surprise.

sites.name: Hippo Regius
sites.text: St Augustine dies during the Vandal siege.

sites.name: Carthage
sites.text: Taken by Gaiseric: capital of the Vandal kingdom until 533.

steps.title: The sack of Rome
steps.text: With Africa's grain and a fleet, the Vandals ruled the western Mediterranean. In June 455 Gaiseric sailed to Rome and plundered it for two weeks, taking the empress and the treasures of the Temple of Jerusalem back to Carthage.

sites.name: Rome
sites.text: Two weeks of plunder by the Vandals.

migrations.name: Angles, Saxons and Jutes
migrations.summary: When Rome left Britain in 410, the Britons hired Saxon soldiers, says Gildas, and the soldiers sent for their kin. Over the fifth and sixth centuries Angles from Schleswig, Saxons from the North Sea coast and Jutes from Jutland settled eastern Britain, and their language became English. Britons fought back, the battle of Mount Badon is remembered as a victory, and some sailed to Armorica, which became Brittany.

steps.label: c. 430 to 500
steps.title: Over the North Sea
steps.text: Small boats like the Nydam ship, rowed, not sailed, carried warriors and then families. They settled Kent, East Anglia, the Thames valley and Lindsey; their cemeteries show the same brooches and pots as at home.

sites.name: Sutton Hoo
sites.text: Later royal ship burial of the East Angles, about 625.

sites.name: Ebbsfleet
sites.text: Where Hengist and Horsa are said to have landed in 449.

steps.label: c. 500 to 600
steps.title: Westward through Britain
steps.text: After a pause, perhaps after Mount Badon, the English pushed west in the later sixth century, to the Severn and up to Northumbria. Britons kept Wales, Cornwall and the north-west, and many crossed the sea to Brittany.

sites.name: Dyrham
sites.text: The West Saxons cut off the Britons of Wales from those of Cornwall.

migrations.name: The Ostrogoths
migrations.summary: The Ostrogoths lived under the Huns until they won their freedom at the Nedao in 454. Settled in Pannonia and then the Balkans, they were a danger on Constantinople's doorstep, until Emperor Zeno sent their king Theodoric to take Italy from Odoacer. After four years of war Theodoric ruled Italy from Ravenna, and his kingdom was the most Roman of them all.

steps.label: 454 to 488
steps.title: Free of the Huns
steps.text: The Ostrogoths settled in Pannonia, then moved into the Balkans in 473, now allies, now enemies of the eastern emperor. Their young king Theodoric had grown up a hostage in Constantinople.

sites.name: Novae
sites.text: Theodoric's base on the Danube.

steps.label: 488 to 493
steps.title: Theodoric takes Italy
steps.text: In the autumn of 488 the whole people, perhaps 100,000, set out with their wagons for Italy. They beat Odoacer on the Isonzo and at Verona in 489, besieged him in Ravenna for three years and, in 493, Theodoric killed him with his own hand at a banquet.

sites.name: Ravenna
sites.text: Theodoric's capital; his mausoleum and churches still stand.

sites.name: Verona
sites.text: Theodoric beats Odoacer: the "Dietrich of Bern" of German legend.

migrations.name: The Lombards
migrations.summary: The Lombards, the "long beards", moved from the middle Danube into Pannonia in the sixth century. In 568, after destroying the Gepids with the Avars, King Alboin led his whole people, with Saxons and others, into an Italy worn out by Justinian's wars and plague. They took the north and much of the south; Lombardy still bears their name.

steps.label: 489 to 567
steps.title: To Pannonia
steps.text: The Lombards moved into the lands north of the Danube left empty by the Rugii, then in 526 into Pannonia. Allied with the Avars, they destroyed the Gepids in 567; Alboin made a drinking cup of the Gepid king's skull.

steps.label: 568 to 572
steps.title: Into Italy
steps.text: At Easter 568 they left Pannonia to the Avars and crossed the Julian Alps. Cividale fell first, then Milan in 569; Pavia held out for three years and became their capital.

sites.name: Pavia
sites.text: Lombard capital until Charlemagne took it in 774.

migrations.name: The Slavic migrations
migrations.summary: In the sixth and seventh centuries Slavic peoples spread from a homeland between the Vistula and the Dnieper over half of Europe: west to the Elbe, south over the Danube deep into the Balkans and Greece, and north into the forests toward Novgorod. Simple farming villages of sunken houses mark their spread. They are the ancestors of today's Poles, Czechs, Serbs, Croats, Bulgarians, Russians and Ukrainians.

steps.label: c. 500 to 600
steps.title: West to the Elbe
steps.text: As the Germanic peoples left for the empire, Slavs settled their old lands, reaching Bohemia and the Elbe by about 600.

sites.name: Prague-Korchak
sites.text: The early Slavic culture of simple villages and plain pots.

steps.label: c. 550 to 630
steps.title: Over the Danube
steps.text: Slav raiders crossed the Danube from the 540s, and then settled in the Balkans as the Avars broke the Roman frontier. They reached the Peloponnese; Croats and Serbs arrived in the 620s.

steps.label: c. 600 to 700
steps.title: North into the forests
steps.text: Eastern Slavs moved north up the rivers into the lands of the Finnic and Baltic peoples, reaching Lake Ilmen, where Novgorod would rise.

migrations.name: The Avars
migrations.summary: The Avars were horsemen from the steppe, perhaps the remnant of the Rouran khaganate of Mongolia, destroyed by the Turks in 552. Fleeing west, they reached the Caucasus in 557, took Roman gold to fight Rome's enemies, and in 568 seized the Hungarian plain. For 230 years their khagans ruled the Slavs and raided the empire, until Charlemagne broke them.

steps.label: 555 to 562
steps.title: Fleeing the Turks
steps.text: The Avars rode across the steppe to the north Caucasus and sent envoys to Justinian, who paid them to fight other nomads. The Turks complained the Avars were their runaway slaves.

steps.label: 567 to 568
steps.title: Into Pannonia
steps.text: With the Lombards they destroyed the Gepids in 567; the next year the Lombards left for Italy and the Avars took the whole Carpathian basin.

sites.name: Avar ring
sites.text: The khagans' great camp, plundered by Charlemagne's Franks in 796.

migrations.name: The Hijra
migrations.summary: Persecuted in Mecca, some of the first Muslims crossed the Red Sea to the Christian king of Aksum in 615. In 622 Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for Yathrib, which became Medina, "the city of the Prophet". This migration, the Hijra, is the start of the Islamic calendar.

steps.title: Refuge in Aksum
steps.text: About eighty Muslims crossed to Ethiopia, where the Negus refused to hand them back to Mecca.

sites.name: Aksum
sites.text: The Christian kingdom that gave the first Muslims refuge.

steps.title: From Mecca to Medina
steps.text: Muhammad and Abu Bakr slipped out of Mecca, hid three days in a cave on Mount Thawr, and reached Yathrib about 400 km to the north. There the first Muslim community was formed.

sites.name: Mecca
sites.text: Muhammad leaves his home city.

sites.name: Medina
sites.text: The first Muslim community; Muhammad's mosque and tomb.

migrations.name: The Bulgars
migrations.summary: The Bulgars were Turkic horsemen of the steppe north of the Black Sea. When the Khazars broke their "Old Great Bulgaria" after Khan Kubrat died, his sons led their people in different directions. Asparukh crossed the Danube and founded a Bulgarian state in 681; his people mixed with the Slavs there and took their language. Another branch went north to the Volga.

steps.label: 632 to 668
steps.title: Old Great Bulgaria
steps.text: Kubrat freed the Bulgars from the Avars and ruled the steppe east of the Sea of Azov. After his death the Khazars pressed in from the east.

sites.name: Phanagoria
sites.text: Kubrat's capital on the Taman peninsula.

steps.label: 670 to 700
steps.title: Asparukh and the Danube
steps.text: Asparukh led his horde west to the Danube delta and, after beating a Byzantine army in 680, crossed into today's Bulgaria. Byzantium recognised his state in 681. Kotrag's Bulgars went north and founded Volga Bulgaria.

sites.name: Pliska
sites.text: First capital of the Bulgarian state.

migrations.name: The Magyars
migrations.summary: The Hungarians, the Magyars, speak a language whose closest kin are spoken in western Siberia. Over centuries their ancestors moved from the Ural forests onto the steppe and west along it. In 895, under Arpad, seven tribes crossed the Carpathians and took the plain that is Hungary still. For sixty years their horsemen raided Europe, from Spain to Constantinople, until Otto I beat them at the Lech in 955.

steps.label: c. 750 to 890
steps.title: Along the steppe
steps.text: From "Magna Hungaria" near the Urals the Magyars moved to Levedia by the Don and then to Etelkoz between the Dnieper and the Danube, living alongside the Khazars as herders and horsemen.

sites.name: Magna Hungaria
sites.text: The Magyars' old home on the edge of the Urals, where a Dominican friar found Hungarian speakers in 1235.

steps.label: 895 to 900
steps.title: The Conquest
steps.text: Attacked by the Pechenegs, the seven tribes crossed the Verecke pass in 895 and took the Carpathian basin from Bulgars, Moravians and Slavs. Hungarians call it the honfoglalas, the "taking of the homeland".

sites.name: Verecke Pass
sites.text: The pass over the Carpathians where the Magyars entered their new land.

steps.label: 899 to 955
steps.title: The raids
steps.text: Magyar riders struck Italy, Germany, France, even Spain, faster than any army could follow. "From the arrows of the Hungarians, deliver us, O Lord," prayed the monks. In 955 Otto I destroyed their army on the Lechfeld near Augsburg.

sites.name: Lechfeld
sites.text: Otto I crushes the Magyar army; they settle down and become a Christian kingdom.

migrations.name: The Norse settlers
migrations.summary: The Viking Age was raids, but also one of the great migrations of the Middle Ages. Norwegians settled the islands of the North Atlantic, Iceland and Greenland, and touched America; Danes settled the Danelaw in England and Normandy in France; Swedes went east along the rivers of Russia, where the Rus' founded the first Russian state.

steps.label: 750 to 900
steps.title: The Rus' go east
steps.text: Swedish traders and warriors, the Varangians, rowed up the Gulf of Finland to Staraya Ladoga, then down the Volga and the Dnieper to Baghdad's silver and Constantinople. Rurik ruled Novgorod from 862, and Oleg took Kiev in 882.

sites.name: Staraya Ladoga
sites.text: The first Norse trading town in Russia.

sites.name: Kiev
sites.text: Capital of Kievan Rus'.

steps.label: 790 to 870
steps.title: Islands and the Danelaw
steps.text: After the first raids, Norwegians settled the Shetlands, Orkneys, Hebrides and founded Dublin in 841. The Danish Great Heathen Army landed in 865, took York and settled half of England, the Danelaw.

sites.name: Dublin
sites.text: Founded as a Norse longphort, a ship camp, in 841.

sites.name: Jorvik
sites.text: York, capital of the Viking kingdom of Northumbria.

steps.label: 870 to 930
steps.title: Iceland and Normandy
steps.text: From about 870 Norwegian families fleeing King Harald Finehair sailed to Iceland; in sixty years it was full, and in 930 they founded the Althing, a parliament. In 911 the Frankish king gave Rouen to the Viking chief Rollo: Normandy.

sites.name: Thingvellir
sites.text: Where the Icelanders met in the Althing from 930.

sites.name: Rouen
sites.text: Given to Rollo: the start of Normandy.

steps.label: 985 to 1010
steps.title: Greenland and Vinland
steps.text: Erik the Red, outlawed from Iceland, led 25 ships to Greenland in 985; 14 arrived. About 1000 his son Leif Eriksson reached the coast of North America, Vinland. The settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows did not last; the Greenland Norse held on for four centuries.

sites.name: Brattahlid
sites.text: Erik the Red's farm in Greenland.

sites.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
sites.text: The only known Norse site in North America.

migrations.name: The Turks move west
migrations.summary: In the eleventh century Turkic horsemen poured west out of Central Asia. The Oghuz Turks led by the Seljuk clan took Iran and Baghdad, and after Manzikert in 1071 their herds and families filled Anatolia, which in time became Turkey. To the north, the Kipchaks (Cumans) spread over the whole steppe from the Irtysh to the Danube.

steps.label: 985 to 1040
steps.title: The Oghuz cross the Oxus
steps.text: Seljuk, a chief of the Oghuz on the lower Syr Darya, became a Muslim about 985. His grandsons Tughril and Chaghri led their tribes into Khorasan and beat the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040.

sites.name: Dandanaqan
sites.text: The Seljuks win Khorasan from the Ghaznavids.

steps.label: 1030 to 1080
steps.title: The Kipchaks on the steppe
steps.text: From the Irtysh, the Kipchaks pushed west across the steppe, driving the Pechenegs and Oghuz before them. Russians called them Polovtsians, Byzantines Cumans; their lands became the Dasht-i Kipchak, the Kipchak steppe.

steps.label: 1040 to 1071
steps.title: Iran and Baghdad
steps.text: Tughril took Iran, entered Baghdad in 1055 as protector of the caliph, and was named sultan. Turkmen herders roamed ahead of the armies into Armenia and Anatolia.

sites.name: Baghdad
sites.text: Tughril becomes sultan, guardian of the Abbasid caliph.

sites.name: Manzikert
sites.text: Alp Arslan captures the Byzantine emperor; Anatolia opens to the Turks.

steps.label: 1071 to 1100
steps.title: Into Anatolia
steps.text: After Manzikert Turkmen tribes moved in with their flocks. The Seljuks of Rum ruled from Nicaea, then from Konya.

sites.name: Konya
sites.text: Capital of the Seljuk sultanate of Rum.

migrations.name: The Fulani across the Sahel
migrations.summary: The Fulani, cattle herders of the Senegal valley, spread east across the whole Sahel over eight centuries, grazing their herds between farming peoples, from Senegal to Cameroon. Many became devout Muslim scholars; in the jihads of the 1700s and 1800s Fulani leaders founded states, the greatest the Sokoto Caliphate of Usman dan Fodio.

steps.label: c. 1000 to 1500
steps.title: East from Futa Toro
steps.text: Herding families moved east by stages along the band of grassland between the desert and the forest, to Macina on the inner Niger delta and on to Hausaland.

steps.label: 1500 to 1810
steps.title: To Adamawa, and the jihad
steps.text: Fulani herders reached Bornu and Adamawa in Cameroon. In 1804 Usman dan Fodio proclaimed a jihad against the Hausa kings and founded the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest state in West Africa.

sites.name: Sokoto
sites.text: Capital of Usman dan Fodio's caliphate.

migrations.name: The Romani migration
migrations.summary: The Romani people came from north-western India: their language is close to Punjabi and Hindi. They left about the year 1000, perhaps as camp followers driven by the wars of Mahmud of Ghazni, and moved through Persia and Armenia into the Byzantine Empire. In the fifteenth century they spread across all of Europe, where they were called "Egyptians", the root of "Gypsies".

steps.label: c. 1000 to 1300
steps.title: Out of India
steps.text: Words borrowed from Persian, Armenian and Greek in Romani show the road they took, and how long they stayed: long in the Greek-speaking Byzantine world.

steps.label: 1350 to 1505
steps.title: Into Europe
steps.text: Romani appear in Greece and the Balkans in the 1300s. In 1417 a band with a letter from Emperor Sigismund reached Germany; they were in Paris in 1427, Spain by 1425 and Scotland by 1505.

sites.name: Modon
sites.text: A Venetian port in Greece, called "Little Egypt", where travellers met Romani.

sites.name: Paris
sites.text: A Romani band camps at La Chapelle in August 1427.

migrations.name: The Tai peoples move south
migrations.summary: The Tai peoples, ancestors of the Thai, Lao and Shan, came from the hills of today's Guangxi and Guizhou in southern China. Between about 1000 and 1300 they moved south-west down the river valleys into the lands of the Mon and the Khmer, founding kingdoms: Sukhothai and Lanna in Thailand, Lan Xang in Laos, the Shan states of Burma, and the Ahom kingdom in Assam.

steps.label: c. 1000 to 1200
steps.title: Down the valleys
steps.text: Rice farmers organised in muang, valley chiefdoms, moved south and west, pushed perhaps by Chinese expansion and drawn by open land.

steps.label: 1200 to 1350
steps.title: New kingdoms
steps.text: Tai chiefs threw off Khmer rule at Sukhothai about 1238; Mangrai founded Chiang Mai in 1296; Sukaphaa led the Ahom over the mountains into Assam in 1228; Fa Ngum founded Lan Xang in 1353.

sites.name: Sukhothai
sites.text: The first great Thai kingdom.

migrations.name: The Thule (Inuit) migration
migrations.summary: The ancestors of the Inuit, the Thule people, came out of Alaska about 1000 and crossed the whole Canadian Arctic to Greenland in perhaps two centuries, with dog sleds, kayaks, big skin boats and harpoons for whales. They replaced the older Dorset people and met the Norse in Greenland. Every Inuit people from Alaska to Greenland descends from them.

steps.label: c. 1000 to 1200
steps.title: Across the Arctic
steps.text: Following the bowhead whales in a warm spell, the Thule moved east along the northern coasts and the channels between the Arctic islands, faster than any people before them.

steps.label: c. 1200 to 1350
steps.title: Into Greenland
steps.text: They crossed Smith Sound into Greenland and moved down both coasts, meeting the Norse farmers, whom they called Kavdlunait. By the time the Norse colony died out in the 1400s, the Inuit held all of Greenland.

sites.name: Smith Sound
sites.text: The narrows between Canada and Greenland.

migrations.name: The Banu Hilal
migrations.summary: In about 1050 the Fatimid caliph of Egypt, to punish his rebellious vassals in Ifriqiya, let loose on them the Bedouin tribes of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym. Some 200,000 Arabs with their camels moved west across North Africa, sacked Kairouan in 1057 and spread over the plains of the Maghreb. They did more than the first conquest to make North Africa Arabic-speaking.

steps.label: 1050 to 1057
steps.title: Out of Egypt
steps.text: The tribes crossed Cyrenaica and Tripolitania and beat the Zirid army at Haydaran in 1052. Kairouan was abandoned to them in 1057.

sites.name: Kairouan
sites.text: The old capital of Ifriqiya, sacked by the Bedouin.

steps.label: 1060 to 1160
steps.title: Across the Maghreb
steps.text: The tribes spread west over the high plains of Algeria. The Almohads moved many of them on into Morocco. Ibn Khaldun later compared them to a swarm of locusts; others credit their epic, the Taghriba, which is still sung.

migrations.name: The Vietnamese march south
migrations.summary: For seven centuries the Vietnamese pushed south from the Red River delta along the narrow coast, the Nam tien, "march to the south". Soldier-farmers settled the lands of Champa and then of the Khmer, until Vietnam reached the Mekong delta and took the shape it has today.

steps.label: 1069 to 1471
steps.title: Taking Champa
steps.text: Vietnamese kings took Cham provinces in 1069 and 1306 (Hue came as a princess's dowry) and in 1471 Le Thanh Tong sacked Vijaya, the Cham capital.

sites.name: Vijaya
sites.text: Capital of Champa, sacked in 1471.

steps.label: 1611 to 1757
steps.title: To the Mekong
steps.text: The Nguyen lords pushed on to the southern coast, then settled Prey Nokor, a Khmer port, which became Saigon in 1698. By 1757 they held the whole Mekong delta.

sites.name: Saigon
sites.text: The Khmer port of Prey Nokor, made a Vietnamese prefecture in 1698.

migrations.name: Jews move to Poland and Lithuania
migrations.summary: The Jews of the Rhineland, the first Ashkenazim, suffered massacres in the First Crusade in 1096 and later in the Black Death. England expelled its Jews in 1290 and France in 1306. Polish kings, starting with the charter of Kalisz in 1264, welcomed them as townspeople and traders. By 1500 Poland and Lithuania held the largest Jewish community in the world, and Yiddish, born on the Rhine, was its language.

steps.label: 1096 to 1306
steps.title: Massacres and expulsions in the west
steps.text: Crusaders on their way east murdered the Jews of Worms, Mainz and Speyer in 1096. Expelled from England and France, Jews moved to Germany and on east.

sites.name: Mainz
sites.text: One of the three great Jewish communities of the Rhine, attacked in 1096.

steps.label: 1264 to 1500
steps.title: The charter of Kalisz
steps.text: Boleslaw the Pious's charter of 1264, and Casimir the Great after the Black Death, protected Jews in Poland. Jewish towns grew in Krakow, Lviv, Lublin, Grodno and Vilnius.

sites.name: Kalisz
sites.text: Where Duke Boleslaw granted the Jews their charter.

migrations.name: The Mexica migration
migrations.summary: The Mexica told how they left Aztlan, an island in a lake somewhere in the north-west, in about 1111, led by their god Huitzilopochtli. They wandered for two centuries, settling and leaving, until they saw an eagle on a cactus on an island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there in 1325. The eagle is on Mexico's flag today.

steps.label: c. 1111 to 1250
steps.title: From Aztlan
steps.text: Where Aztlan lay no one knows; the story is part legend. The codices show the Mexica walking, carrying their god, through Chicomoztoc, the place of the seven caves, and Coatepec near Tula.

sites.name: Coatepec
sites.text: Where, in legend, Huitzilopochtli was born and fought his sister.

steps.label: c. 1250 to 1325
steps.title: To the lake
steps.text: Arriving in the Valley of Mexico, the Mexica were despised newcomers, mercenaries for the city of Culhuacan, driven from Chapultepec. On a swampy island they found the eagle on the cactus.

sites.name: Tenochtitlan
sites.text: Founded on an island in Lake Texcoco; today Mexico City.

migrations.name: German settlers in the east
migrations.summary: From the twelfth century, lords and churchmen in the lands east of the Elbe invited farmers, miners and townsmen from Flanders, the Rhineland, Saxony and Franconia, offering land and German town law. Hundreds of thousands moved east over two centuries, into Brandenburg, Pomerania, Silesia, Bohemia, Prussia and as far as Transylvania. The Ostsiedlung changed the map of languages in Europe until 1945.

steps.label: 1140 to 1250
steps.title: East of the Elbe
steps.text: Settlers cleared forest and drained marsh in Holstein, Mecklenburg and Brandenburg; Slavic princes in Pomerania and Silesia invited them too. New towns like Lubeck (1143) and Berlin grew.

sites.name: Lubeck
sites.text: Founded 1143; later queen of the Hanseatic League.

steps.label: 1141 to 1350
steps.title: To Prussia and Transylvania
steps.text: King Geza II of Hungary invited settlers, mostly from the Moselle, to Transylvania, where the "Saxons" built fortified churches. In the 1200s the Teutonic Knights brought colonists into conquered Prussia, founding Thorn, Kulm and Konigsberg.

sites.name: Hermannstadt
sites.text: Sibiu, chief town of the Transylvanian Saxons.

sites.name: Konigsberg
sites.text: Founded by the Teutonic Knights.

migrations.name: The Navajo and Apache go south
migrations.summary: The Navajo and Apache speak Athabaskan languages, whose relatives are spoken in Alaska and north-western Canada. Some time between about 1300 and 1500 their ancestors made a journey of 3,000 km down the plains along the Rocky Mountains to the Southwest, where they became the neighbours of the Pueblo peoples.

steps.label: c. 1300 to 1450
steps.title: Down the Rockies
steps.text: Small bands of hunters with dog travois moved south along the eastern side of the mountains.

steps.label: c. 1450 to 1525
steps.title: The Southwest
steps.text: By the early 1500s they were in the Southwest, when the Spanish first met "Apaches de Nabajo". The Navajo learned farming and weaving from the Pueblos, and later sheep-herding from the Spanish.

sites.name: Dinetah
sites.text: The first homeland of the Navajo in the Southwest.

migrations.name: The expulsions from Spain
migrations.summary: In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella ordered every Jew in Spain to convert or leave. Perhaps 100,000 or more left, to Portugal (which forced them to convert in 1497), to North Africa, Italy and above all the Ottoman Empire, where Sultan Bayezid II welcomed them. Their descendants, the Sephardim, kept their Spanish, Ladino, for 500 years. Between 1609 and 1614 Spain also expelled some 300,000 Moriscos, descendants of its Muslims.

steps.label: 1492 to 1500
steps.title: The Alhambra Decree
steps.text: Jews had four months to sell what they could and go. Ships took them from Cadiz and Cartagena to Fez, Naples, Salonica and Constantinople; Salonica became a mostly Jewish city.

sites.name: Granada
sites.text: Where the decree was signed, three months after the city fell.

sites.name: Salonica
sites.text: The "Jerusalem of the Balkans", home of the Sephardim until 1943.

steps.label: 1609 to 1614
steps.title: The Moriscos
steps.text: Philip III expelled the Moriscos, Muslims forcibly converted a century before. From Valencia and Aragon ships carried them to Oran and Tunis; in Morocco some founded the corsair republic of Sale.

sites.name: Valencia
sites.text: A third of the kingdom's people were Moriscos.

migrations.name: The Atlantic slave trade
migrations.summary: Over three and a half centuries some 12.5 million Africans were packed into ships and carried across the Atlantic; about two million died on the Middle Passage. Most were taken to work sugar, coffee and cotton in Brazil and the Caribbean; about 400,000 to North America. It was the largest forced migration in history, and it made the Americas, and Africa, what they are.
migrations.numbers: 12.5 million people taken; 10.7 million survived the crossing

steps.label: 1501 to 1580
steps.title: The first crossings
steps.text: The first enslaved Africans reached Hispaniola in 1501 to replace the dying Taino. From the 1530s the trade grew with the sugar mills of Portuguese Brazil, fed from the Bight of Benin and the Kongo.

sites.name: Elmina
sites.text: Portuguese fortress of 1482 on the Gold Coast, later a great slave castle.

sites.name: Salvador da Bahia
sites.text: Brazil's first capital, built on the sugar of the enslaved.

steps.label: 1575 to 1700
steps.title: Angola, sugar and the islands
steps.text: From Luanda, founded in 1576, the Portuguese shipped millions from Angola and the Kongo to Rio and Bahia. In the 1600s the English, Dutch and French built sugar islands: Barbados, Jamaica and Saint-Domingue.

sites.name: Luanda
sites.text: From here more Africans were shipped than from any other port.

sites.name: Barbados
sites.text: The first great English sugar island.

steps.label: 1700 to 1807
steps.title: The height of the trade
steps.text: In the 1700s over six million people were shipped, more than in all other centuries together. Ships from Liverpool, Nantes and Rhode Island carried them; rice and tobacco planters of Carolina and Virginia bought them in Charleston.

sites.name: Charleston
sites.text: Nearly half of all enslaved Africans brought to North America landed here.

sites.name: Saint-Domingue
sites.text: The richest colony on earth, worked by half a million enslaved people, until the revolution of 1791.

steps.label: 1807 to 1866
steps.title: Abolition
steps.text: Britain banned the trade in 1807 and the United States in 1808, and the Royal Navy hunted slave ships off Africa. Brazil stopped in 1850; the last known voyage reached Cuba in 1866. Slavery itself ended in Brazil only in 1888.

sites.name: Freetown
sites.text: Where the Royal Navy freed the Africans it took from slave ships.

migrations.name: European settlers in the Americas
migrations.summary: In the three centuries after Columbus, perhaps two million Europeans crossed to the Americas: Spaniards to Mexico and Peru, Portuguese to Brazil, English and Scots to Virginia and New England, French to the St Lawrence, Dutch to the Hudson. Most early colonists were young men, many of them indentured servants; the English colonies drew whole families. They came with the diseases that killed most of the native peoples.

steps.label: 1502 to 1600
steps.title: Spain and Portugal
steps.text: From Seville, the only port allowed to trade with the Indies, some 250,000 Spaniards sailed in the 1500s, most to Mexico and Peru. Portuguese settled Brazil's sugar coast from the 1530s.

sites.name: Veracruz
sites.text: Where Cortes landed and where the treasure fleets loaded silver.

sites.name: Olinda
sites.text: Capital of Pernambuco, Brazil's first rich sugar colony.

steps.label: 1607 to 1640
steps.title: Jamestown, Quebec and Plymouth
steps.text: The English founded Jamestown in 1607, the French Quebec in 1608, the Pilgrims Plymouth in 1620, and the Dutch New Amsterdam in 1625. In the Great Migration of the 1630s some 20,000 Puritans came to New England.

sites.name: Jamestown
sites.text: The first lasting English colony in America.

sites.name: Quebec
sites.text: Founded by Samuel de Champlain.

sites.name: Plymouth
sites.text: Founded by the Pilgrims of the Mayflower.

steps.label: 1700 to 1775
steps.title: Germans, Scots and Irish
steps.text: In the 1700s new settlers poured into British America: Germans from the Palatinate to Pennsylvania, Scots and Ulster Scots to the back country. By 1775 the thirteen colonies held two and a half million people.

sites.name: Philadelphia
sites.text: The great port of entry for Germans and Ulster Scots.

migrations.name: The Oromo migrations
migrations.summary: In the 1500s the Oromo, cattle-herding peoples of the southern Ethiopian highlands, moved north and east in great waves, organised by their gadaa system, in which a new generation of warriors took power every eight years. While the Christian empire and the Adal sultanate exhausted each other in war, the Oromo filled the lands between, and today they are the largest people of Ethiopia.

steps.label: 1522 to 1570
steps.title: Out of the south
steps.text: From their home around Mount Walabu in Bale, the Borana and Barentu Oromo moved into the lands emptied by the war between Ethiopia and Adal, toward Harar and the Awash.

sites.name: Harar
sites.text: The walled city of the emirs of Adal, besieged by the Oromo.

steps.label: 1570 to 1618
steps.title: To the heart of Ethiopia
steps.text: The Oromo spread over Shewa, Wollo and the west, reaching Gojjam and the Abay. The emperors could not stop them and moved their court north to Gondar.

migrations.name: The Russians cross Siberia
migrations.summary: In 1582 the Cossack Yermak, hired by the Stroganov merchants, crossed the Urals and took the Tatar khanate of Sibir. In sixty years Cossacks and fur traders went 6,000 km east by river and portage to the Pacific, founding forts that became cities. Peasants, exiles and Old Believers followed them; by 1700 there were more Russians than natives in Siberia.

steps.label: 1582 to 1620
steps.title: Over the Urals
steps.text: Yermak's 840 men took Isker, the khan's capital, in 1582. Tobolsk was founded in 1587, Tomsk in 1604, Yeniseysk in 1619: each a stockade on a river, collecting furs as tribute.

sites.name: Tobolsk
sites.text: First capital of Russian Siberia.

steps.label: 1620 to 1700
steps.title: To the Pacific
steps.text: Cossacks reached the Lena and founded Yakutsk in 1632; Ivan Moskvitin reached the Sea of Okhotsk in 1639. Others went down the Amur until China stopped them, and in 1697 Vladimir Atlasov took Kamchatka.

sites.name: Yakutsk
sites.text: Fort on the Lena; the fur capital of eastern Siberia.

sites.name: Okhotsk
sites.text: The first Russian port on the Pacific.

migrations.name: The Kalmyks' long ride
migrations.summary: The Kalmyks, a Mongol people of the Oirat confederation, Buddhists, left Dzungaria early in the 1600s and rode 3,000 km west to the lower Volga, where they founded a khanate under the Russian tsars. In the winter of 1771, chafing under Russia, most of them, some 150,000 people, set out to ride home; harried by Kazakhs and Cossacks, fewer than half reached China.

steps.label: 1608 to 1632
steps.title: West to the Volga
steps.text: Pressed by their rivals among the Oirats and short of pasture, the Torghut Kalmyks under Kho Orluk crossed the Kazakh steppe and reached the Volga about 1630.

sites.name: Kalmyk khanate
sites.text: The only Buddhist state in Europe, on the steppe of the lower Volga.

steps.title: The flight east
steps.text: In January 1771 Khan Ubashi led 33,000 households east across the frozen steppe; the Kalmyks west of the unfrozen Volga were left behind. Those who reached Ili were resettled by the Qianlong emperor.

sites.name: Ili
sites.text: Where the survivors were received by the Qing.

migrations.name: The Huguenot refuge
migrations.summary: In 1685 Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes and outlawed Protestantism in France. Though leaving was forbidden, some 200,000 Huguenots escaped, to the Netherlands, England, Switzerland, Prussia and as far as the Cape of Good Hope. They took their skills with them: silk weaving to London, watchmaking to Geneva; a third of Berlin was French by 1700.

steps.label: 1685 to 1687
steps.title: The great flight
steps.text: Huguenots crossed the borders at night, disguised as peasants or hidden in barrels on ships. They went to Holland, "the great ark of the refugees", to Geneva, and to London, where Spitalfields filled with silk weavers.

sites.name: Spitalfields
sites.text: Huguenot silk weavers fill this corner of London.

steps.label: 1688 to 1700
steps.title: Berlin and the Cape
steps.text: The Elector of Brandenburg's Edict of Potsdam offered refugees land, tax freedom and their own churches; some 20,000 came. In 1688 the Dutch East India Company took about 200 to the Cape, where they planted vines at Franschhoek.

sites.name: Franschhoek
sites.text: "French corner": Huguenot vineyards at the Cape.

sites.name: Berlin
sites.text: One in three Berliners was a French refugee by 1700.

migrations.name: Convicts and settlers to Australia
migrations.summary: In 1788 the First Fleet landed 750 convicts at Sydney Cove, on land the Eora people had lived on for tens of thousands of years. Britain transported some 162,000 convicts to Australia until 1868. Free settlers came too, and after gold was found in 1851 they came in floods: Australia's population tripled in ten years.

steps.label: 1787 to 1830
steps.title: The First Fleet
steps.text: Eleven ships sailed from Portsmouth in May 1787 by Tenerife, Rio and the Cape, eight months and 24,000 km, and anchored in Botany Bay in January 1788. Governor Phillip moved on to Sydney Cove.

sites.name: Sydney Cove
sites.text: The convict colony of New South Wales, founded 26 January 1788.

sites.name: Van Diemen's Land
sites.text: Tasmania, where the worst offenders were sent.

steps.label: 1830 to 1868
steps.title: Free settlers and gold
steps.text: Assisted passages brought poor British and Irish families. The gold rushes of Victoria from 1851 drew diggers from everywhere; Melbourne became one of the richest cities in the world. The last convict ship reached Western Australia in 1868.

sites.name: Ballarat
sites.text: The gold fields of Victoria, and the Eureka rebellion of 1854.

migrations.name: The Mfecane
migrations.summary: In the 1810s and 1820s the rise of Shaka's Zulu kingdom, drought and the slave trade set off a chain of wars and migrations across southern Africa, the Mfecane, "the crushing". Peoples fled, fought and remade themselves: Mzilikazi's Ndebele went north to Zimbabwe, Zwangendaba's Ngoni went 3,000 km to Lake Tanganyika, Sebetwane's Kololo to the Zambezi, and Moshoeshoe gathered refugees into the Basotho nation.

steps.label: 1818 to 1835
steps.title: Flight from the Zulu
steps.text: Zwangendaba and Soshangane, beaten by Shaka's ally turned rival, led their followers north into Mozambique. Mzilikazi broke with Shaka in 1823 and moved onto the highveld.

sites.name: Zulu kingdom
sites.text: Shaka built a powerful army and state here from 1818.

steps.label: 1835 to 1848
steps.title: North over the Zambezi
steps.text: The Ngoni crossed the Zambezi on 19 November 1835, a date fixed by an eclipse, and went on to Lake Tanganyika. Driven by the Boers, Mzilikazi's Ndebele moved north to found Bulawayo's kingdom.

sites.name: Ufipa
sites.text: Where Zwangendaba died, far from where he set out.

migrations.name: The great Atlantic migration
migrations.summary: Between 1820 and 1924 some 55 million Europeans crossed the Atlantic, the largest voluntary migration in history: Irish fleeing famine, Germans and Scandinavians seeking land, Italians, Poles and Jews from the Russian Empire seeking work and freedom. Most went to the United States; millions to Argentina, Brazil and Canada. Steamships cut the crossing from six weeks to one, until the United States closed its doors in 1924.

steps.label: 1820 to 1845
steps.title: The first wave
steps.text: Sailing ships carried British, Irish and German emigrants from Liverpool and Le Havre, often in the holds that carried cotton the other way.

steps.label: 1845 to 1880
steps.title: Famine and revolution
steps.text: The Great Famine drove a million and a half Irish to America in ten years, many on "coffin ships". After the failed revolutions of 1848 Germans came in hundreds of thousands, and Scandinavians filled the Midwest.

sites.name: Cobh
sites.text: Queenstown, last sight of Ireland for millions of emigrants.

sites.name: Castle Garden
sites.text: New York's immigrant station before Ellis Island.

steps.label: 1880 to 1914
steps.title: The new immigrants
steps.text: Now the emigrants came from the south and east: Italians, Poles, Greeks, Hungarians and Jews. Ellis Island opened in 1892; in 1907 alone 1.3 million people entered the United States. Italians and Spaniards made Buenos Aires.

sites.name: Ellis Island
sites.text: Through which 12 million immigrants passed, 1892 to 1954.

sites.name: Buenos Aires
sites.text: By 1914 half its people were born abroad.

steps.label: 1914 to 1924
steps.title: The door closes
steps.text: The First World War halted the flow; afterwards, the United States passed quota laws in 1921 and 1924 that all but shut out southern and eastern Europeans. The age of mass migration across the Atlantic was over.

sites.name: Washington
sites.text: The Immigration Act of 1924 sets national quotas.

migrations.name: The Trail of Tears
migrations.summary: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced the Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Seminole off their lands in the American South to "Indian Territory", today's Oklahoma. Some 60,000 people were marched west, many in winter; thousands died of cold, hunger and disease on the way. The Cherokee remember it as "the trail where they cried".

steps.label: 1831 to 1837
steps.title: Choctaw and Creek
steps.text: The Choctaw went first, in 1831 to 1833, in a winter of blizzards. The Creek were removed in chains after the war of 1836.

steps.label: 1838 to 1839
steps.title: The Cherokee
steps.text: In 1838 US troops rounded up 16,000 Cherokee into camps and sent them west in detachments across Tennessee, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri and Arkansas. About 4,000 died.

sites.name: New Echota
sites.text: Cherokee capital in Georgia, emptied by the removal.

sites.name: Tahlequah
sites.text: New capital of the Cherokee Nation in Indian Territory.

migrations.name: Indian indentured labourers
migrations.summary: When the British Empire ended slavery in 1834, planters turned to India. Over 1.3 million Indians signed five-year contracts of indenture, many tricked or desperate, and sailed to the sugar colonies: Mauritius, Guyana, Trinidad, Natal, Fiji. Gandhi fought for them in South Africa. Today their descendants are half the people of Mauritius, Guyana and Trinidad.

steps.label: 1834 to 1860
steps.title: To Mauritius and the Caribbean
steps.text: The first ships left Calcutta for Mauritius in 1834 and for British Guiana in 1838. The voyage to the Caribbean round the Cape took three months.

sites.name: Aapravasi Ghat
sites.text: Immigration depot in Port Louis where half a million Indians landed.

steps.label: 1860 to 1920
steps.title: Natal and Fiji
steps.text: From 1860 Indians were shipped from Madras to Natal's sugar fields, and from 1879 to Fiji. Indenture was abolished in 1917 to 1920 after a long campaign in India.

sites.name: Durban
sites.text: Where Gandhi began his struggle for the rights of Indians.

migrations.name: The Great Trek
migrations.summary: From 1835 some 12,000 Boer farmers, angry at British rule and the end of slavery in the Cape, loaded their ox wagons and trekked north and east beyond the frontier. They fought the Ndebele and the Zulu, beat Dingane at Blood River in 1838, and founded the republics of Natalia, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal. The trek became the founding story of Afrikaner nationalism.

steps.label: 1835 to 1837
steps.title: Over the Orange River
steps.text: Parties under Louis Tregardt, Hendrik Potgieter, Gerrit Maritz and Piet Retief crossed the Orange River. At Vegkop in 1836 Potgieter's laager of wagons beat off the Ndebele.

sites.name: Vegkop
sites.text: A laager of 50 wagons holds off Mzilikazi's army.

steps.label: 1837 to 1846
steps.title: Natal and the Transvaal
steps.text: Retief led wagons over the Drakensberg into Natal; Dingane had him killed. On 16 December 1838 the Boers beat the Zulu at Blood River. Others moved north to found Potchefstroom and Ohrigstad.

sites.name: Blood River
sites.text: Boers beat Dingane's army; the river ran red.

sites.name: Pietermaritzburg
sites.text: Capital of the Boer republic of Natalia.

migrations.name: The trails west
migrations.summary: From 1841, wagon trains of American families set out from the Missouri on the 3,000 km Oregon Trail. The Mormons, driven out of Illinois, trekked to the Great Salt Lake in 1847; the next year gold was found in California, and in 1849 a hundred thousand "forty-niners" rushed west. Some 400,000 people took the trails before the railroad was finished in 1869, crossing lands that were home to the Lakota, Cheyenne and Shoshone.

steps.label: 1841 to 1846
steps.title: The Oregon Trail
steps.text: Wagon trains left Independence in spring to cross the plains, the Rockies at South Pass and the Blue Mountains before the snows. One in ten died on the way, most of cholera.

sites.name: Independence Rock
sites.text: Emigrants hoped to reach it by 4 July to beat the snows.

sites.name: Oregon City
sites.text: End of the Oregon Trail.

steps.label: 1846 to 1847
steps.title: The Mormon trek
steps.text: After their prophet Joseph Smith was murdered, Brigham Young led the Latter-day Saints out of Nauvoo across Iowa and Nebraska to the valley of the Great Salt Lake, where he said, "This is the place."

sites.name: Salt Lake City
sites.text: Founded by the Mormon pioneers on 24 July 1847.

steps.label: 1849 to 1869
steps.title: Gold, and the railroad
steps.text: In 1849 the gold rush turned the trails into highways. California went from 15,000 settlers to a state of 250,000 in four years. In 1869 the railroads met at Promontory, and the wagon trains were over.

sites.name: Sutter's Mill
sites.text: Where gold was found in January 1848.

sites.name: Promontory
sites.text: The golden spike joins the first railroad across America.

migrations.name: The Chinese go overseas
migrations.summary: From the 1840s, war, rebellion and famine in southern China and the demand for labour abroad sent millions of men from Guangdong and Fujian overseas: to the tin mines and plantations of Malaya and the Dutch Indies, to the gold rushes of California and Australia, to the guano pits of Peru, and to build the Central Pacific Railroad. Most meant to return; many stayed, founding the Chinatowns of the world.
migrations.numbers: About 20 million left southern China, 1840 to 1940

steps.label: 1848 to 1882
steps.title: Gold Mountain
steps.text: News of gold in California in 1848 brought tens of thousands from Hong Kong to "Gold Mountain"; they built the western part of the first transcontinental railroad, until the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 shut them out.

sites.name: San Francisco
sites.text: Its Chinatown is the oldest in North America.

steps.label: 1860 to 1930
steps.title: Nanyang, the southern seas
steps.text: Far more went south, to Singapore, Penang, Bangkok, Batavia and Manila, as coolies, traders and miners. By 1930 Chinese were the majority in Singapore and a third of Malaya.

sites.name: Singapore
sites.text: A British port that became a Chinese city.

migrations.name: Crashing into Manchuria
migrations.summary: For two centuries the Qing kept their Manchu homeland closed to Chinese settlers. When the ban crumbled after 1860, peasants from overcrowded, famine-stricken Shandong and Hebei poured north, the Chuang Guandong, "crashing past the pass". Some 25 million came by 1930, by junk across the Bohai Sea and on foot past the Great Wall, and later by railway. It was one of the largest migrations in history.

steps.label: 1860 to 1900
steps.title: Past the pass
steps.text: Settlers walked through Shanhaiguan, where the Great Wall meets the sea, or crossed from the Shandong peninsula to the Liaodong peninsula by boat, and cleared the black-earth plains.

sites.name: Shanhaiguan
sites.text: "The first pass under heaven", where the Great Wall reaches the sea.

steps.label: 1900 to 1930
steps.title: By railway to the north
steps.text: The Russian-built Chinese Eastern Railway and the South Manchuria Railway carried migrants north to Harbin and beyond; in the late 1920s a million came every year, fleeing famine and warlords.

sites.name: Harbin
sites.text: A railway town that grew into a city of half a million.

migrations.name: The Circassian exile
migrations.summary: At the end of a century of war in the Caucasus, the Russian army drove the Circassians and other peoples of the north-west Caucasus from their mountains in 1863 and 1864. Hundreds of thousands were herded to the Black Sea shore and shipped to the Ottoman Empire in overcrowded boats; many died of hunger, cold and disease. Circassians remember it as a genocide; their descendants live in Turkey, Syria and Jordan.

steps.label: 1863 to 1864
steps.title: To the Black Sea shore
steps.text: Russian columns burned the villages valley by valley. The last Circassian resistance ended at Kbaada, today's Krasnaya Polyana above Sochi, in May 1864.

sites.name: Kbaada
sites.text: Russia's victory parade marks the end of the Caucasian War.

steps.label: 1864 to 1865
steps.title: Across the sea
steps.text: From Tuapse, Sochi and Anapa, crowded boats carried the exiles to Trabzon, Samsun and Varna, where tens of thousands died in camps. The Ottomans settled them across Anatolia, the Balkans and Syria.

sites.name: Samsun
sites.text: A port where tens of thousands of exiles died in camps.

migrations.name: Jews leave the Russian Empire
migrations.summary: After the pogroms of 1881 and the harsh May Laws, some two and a half million Jews left the Russian Empire, mostly from the Pale of Settlement, in forty years. Nearly all went to America: New York's Lower East Side became the most crowded place on earth. A few thousand idealists went to Ottoman Palestine to farm, the first waves of Zionist immigration.

steps.label: 1881 to 1914
steps.title: To America
steps.text: Emigrants crossed the German border, often illegally, and took ship at Hamburg and Bremen. Some 2 million reached the United States.

sites.name: Lower East Side
sites.text: New York's Jewish quarter of tenements and garment shops.

steps.label: 1882 to 1914
steps.title: To Palestine
steps.text: In the First and Second Aliyah some 60,000 Jews, many of them young socialists, settled in Ottoman Palestine, founding farming colonies, the first kibbutz at Degania in 1910, and Tel Aviv in 1909.

sites.name: Tel Aviv
sites.text: Founded on the dunes outside Jaffa in 1909.

migrations.name: The Armenian deportations
migrations.summary: In 1915 the Ottoman government ordered the Armenians of Anatolia deported to the Syrian desert. Men were mostly killed at once; women, children and the old were marched for months to Aleppo and Deir ez-Zor. Some 1 million or more died, by massacre, starvation and disease, in what is recognised as the Armenian genocide.

steps.title: The death marches
steps.text: Convoys from Erzurum, Sivas, Harput and the other towns of the east were driven south through the mountains to Aleppo.

sites.name: Erzurum
sites.text: One of the great Armenian centres of the east.

steps.title: Deir ez-Zor
steps.text: From Aleppo the survivors were driven east down the Euphrates to camps around Deir ez-Zor, where most of them were killed or starved in 1916.

sites.name: Deir ez-Zor
sites.text: The end of the deportation routes; a memorial church stood here until 2014.

migrations.name: The Great Migration
migrations.summary: Between 1916 and 1970 some six million African Americans left the rural South, its Jim Crow laws, lynchings and sharecropping, for the cities of the North and West.
