They rode the trains to Chicago, Detroit, New York, Philadelphia and later Los Angeles and Oakland, and changed those cities and America: the Harlem Renaissance, Chicago blues and the civil rights movement grew from it.

steps.label: 1916 to 1940
steps.title: North by train
steps.text: The First World War stopped immigration from Europe and Northern factories needed workers. The Chicago Defender urged Southerners to come; the Illinois Central ran straight up from the Mississippi Delta.

sites.name: Harlem
sites.text: Capital of Black America and its Renaissance.

sites.name: Bronzeville
sites.text: Chicago's "Black Metropolis".

steps.label: 1940 to 1970
steps.title: To the West
steps.text: The Second World War brought a second, larger wave, now also to the shipyards and factories of California.

migrations.name: The Greek and Turkish population exchange
migrations.summary: After Turkey defeated Greece in 1922, Smyrna burned and the Greeks of Anatolia fled. The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 then made it law: Orthodox Christians in Turkey and Muslims in Greece were exchanged, by religion, not by language. About 1.2 million went to Greece and some 400,000 to Turkey, ending 3,000 years of Greek life in Asia Minor.

steps.title: The flight from Smyrna
steps.text: In September 1922 the Turkish army entered Smyrna, the Greek and Armenian quarters burned, and hundreds of thousands crowded the quay waiting for ships.

sites.name: Smyrna
sites.text: The great fire of September 1922; today Izmir.

steps.title: Exchanged by treaty
steps.text: Muslims of Macedonia and Crete were sent to Turkey; Orthodox Christians still in Anatolia, even Turkish speakers, to Greece. Refugees made up a fifth of Greece's people.

sites.name: Lausanne
sites.text: The treaty of January 1923 orders the exchange.

migrations.name: Stalin's deportations
migrations.summary: During the Second World War Stalin deported whole nations he accused of disloyalty: the Volga Germans in 1941, the Chechens, Ingush, Karachays and Balkars, and the Crimean Tatars in 1944, loaded into cattle trucks and sent to Kazakhstan, Central Asia and Siberia. Perhaps a fifth or more died on the way and in the first years. Most could not go home until after Stalin's death, and the Crimean Tatars not until 1989.

steps.title: The Volga Germans
steps.text: Two weeks after Hitler invaded, the Soviet state abolished the Volga German Republic. Some 400,000 people, whose ancestors had come at Catherine the Great's invitation, were sent east.

steps.title: Chechens and Crimean Tatars
steps.text: On 23 February 1944 the whole Chechen and Ingush nations, nearly 500,000 people, were deported in a few days; in May some 190,000 Crimean Tatars were sent to Uzbekistan.

sites.name: Grozny
sites.text: Operation Lentil: the Chechens are deported in a week.

migrations.name: From Mexico to the United States
migrations.summary: In 1942 the United States, short of farm hands in wartime, began the Bracero Program: 4.6 million contracts for Mexican workers by 1964. When it ended, the migrants kept coming, often without papers. By 2010 some 12 million people born in Mexico lived in the United States, the largest single migration of modern times, and Spanish is the country's second language.

steps.label: 1942 to 1964
steps.title: The braceros
steps.text: Workers gathered at recruiting centres in Mexico and were taken north by train to the fields of California, Texas and Arizona.

sites.name: El Paso
sites.text: One of the great crossing points on the border.

steps.label: 1965 to 2020
steps.title: North for work
steps.text: Millions crossed the border to work in farms, building sites and kitchens, from California to Chicago. Since 2008 more Mexicans have gone home than arrived, while Central Americans fleeing violence took the same roads.

sites.name: Los Angeles
sites.text: Home to more Mexicans than any city but Mexico City and Guadalajara.

migrations.name: The flight and expulsion of the Germans
migrations.summary: As the Red Army advanced in 1944 and 1945, millions of Germans fled west from East Prussia, Silesia and Pomerania in winter treks and on ships across the Baltic. After the war the Allies agreed at Potsdam to move the rest out of Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary. Some 12 million people lost their homes, the largest expulsion in European history; Poland itself was moved west, and Poles from the lost east were resettled in the former German lands.

steps.label: 1944 to 1945
steps.title: The treks and the Baltic
steps.text: In January 1945 columns of wagons crossed the frozen Vistula Lagoon under air attack. The navy evacuated about 800,000 people by sea; the Wilhelm Gustloff was sunk with over 9,000 aboard.

sites.name: Wilhelm Gustloff
sites.text: Torpedoed on 30 January 1945: the deadliest sinking in history.

steps.label: 1945 to 1950
steps.title: Expelled
steps.text: After Potsdam, trains carried the remaining Germans west from Silesia, Pomerania and the Sudetenland. Poles expelled from Lwow and Wilno were settled in their place; Breslau became Wroclaw.

sites.name: Wroclaw
sites.text: German Breslau, resettled by Poles, many from Lwow.

migrations.name: Exodus and ingathering, 1948
migrations.summary: In the war of 1947 to 1949 over Palestine and the birth of Israel, some 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes, the Nakba, "catastrophe"; they and their descendants remain refugees in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. In the same years Israel took in hundreds of thousands of Jewish survivors of the Holocaust and, by 1951, whole Jewish communities from Iraq, Yemen and other Arab countries.

steps.label: 1947 to 1949
steps.title: The Palestinian exodus
steps.text: Arabs left Haifa, Jaffa, Lydda, Ramle and hundreds of villages, to Lebanon, the West Bank, Gaza and across the Jordan.

moves.label: To the West Bank and Jordan

sites.name: Lydda
sites.text: Tens of thousands expelled in July 1948.

steps.label: 1948 to 1951
steps.title: Jews come to Israel
steps.text: Holocaust survivors came from the DP camps of Europe; Operation Magic Carpet flew 49,000 Yemeni Jews in 1949 and 1950, and Operation Ezra and Nehemiah airlifted 120,000 Iraqi Jews in 1951.

sites.name: Haifa
sites.text: Port where ships of survivors landed.

migrations.name: The partition of India
migrations.summary: When British India was divided into India and Pakistan in August 1947, some 15 million people crossed the new borders in a few months, Hindus and Sikhs east, Muslims west, in one of the largest migrations in history. Trains arrived full of the dead. Perhaps a million people were killed in the killings that went with it, above all in the Punjab.

steps.label: August to December 1947
steps.title: The Punjab
steps.text: The Radcliffe Line cut the Punjab in two. Columns of refugees, some 400,000 strong, crossed each other on the Grand Trunk Road between Lahore and Amritsar.

sites.name: Wagah
sites.text: The border crossing between Lahore and Amritsar.

steps.label: 1947 to 1948
steps.title: Bengal and Sindh
steps.text: In the east, Hindus left East Bengal for Calcutta and Muslims went the other way, over several years. Muslims from northern India took trains and ships to Karachi, Pakistan's capital.

sites.name: Karachi
sites.text: Pakistan's first capital, its people doubled by refugees.

migrations.name: Coming to postwar Europe
migrations.summary: Rebuilding after 1945, western Europe ran short of workers and looked to its empires and its neighbours. The Windrush brought Caribbean migrants to Britain in 1948, followed by people from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh; West Germany signed guest-worker deals with Italy, Turkey and Yugoslavia; France drew Algerians and Portuguese. When the oil shock of 1973 ended the boom, many stayed and brought their families, and Europe's cities changed for good.

steps.label: 1948 to 1962
steps.title: The Windrush and the empire
steps.text: The Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury in June 1948 with 1,027 passengers, most from Jamaica. Over the next years half a million came from the Caribbean and South Asia.

sites.name: Tilbury
sites.text: Where the Empire Windrush docked on 22 June 1948.

steps.label: 1955 to 1974
steps.title: Guest workers
steps.text: Trains from Istanbul, Belgrade and Naples carried millions of "Gastarbeiter" to Munich and on to the factories of Germany. After Algerian independence in 1962 nearly a million pieds-noirs and many Algerians crossed to France.

sites.name: Munich Hauptbahnhof
sites.text: Arrival hall for guest workers; Germany welcomed its millionth in 1964.

migrations.name: The Vietnamese boat people
migrations.summary: After the fall of Saigon in 1975, and above all in 1978 and 1979, some 800,000 Vietnamese, many of them ethnic Chinese, fled by sea in small, crowded boats. Pirates, storms and hunger killed perhaps 200,000. Survivors reached camps in Malaysia, Hong Kong, Indonesia and the Philippines, and most were resettled in the United States, Canada, Australia and France.

steps.label: 1975 to 1979
steps.title: Escape by sea
steps.text: Families paid in gold for a place on a fishing boat. Malaysia's island of Pulau Bidong held 40,000 people at once.

sites.name: Pulau Bidong
sites.text: A refugee camp on an island off Malaysia.

steps.label: 1979 to 1995
steps.title: New lives
steps.text: An international conference in 1979 agreed to resettle the refugees. Over a million Vietnamese went to new countries; the last camps closed in the 1990s.

sites.name: Little Saigon
sites.text: Westminster, California: the largest Vietnamese community abroad.

migrations.name: The Syrian refugees
migrations.summary: The Syrian civil war that began in 2011 drove half of Syria's people from their homes. Over 6 million fled the country, mostly to Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan. In 2015 about a million people, many of them Syrians, crossed the Aegean in rubber boats and walked up the Balkans to Germany and Sweden, the largest movement of refugees into Europe since 1945.
migrations.numbers: Over 6 million refugees, 6 million more displaced inside Syria

steps.label: 2011 to 2014
steps.title: To the neighbours
steps.text: Refugees crossed into Turkey, Lebanon, where they became a quarter of the people, and Jordan, where the Zaatari camp grew into a city of 80,000.

sites.name: Zaatari
sites.text: Refugee camp in the Jordanian desert.

steps.label: 2015 to 2016
steps.title: The Balkan route
steps.text: From the Turkish coast, smugglers sent people across to Lesbos in rubber boats. They walked and rode through Greece, North Macedonia, Serbia, Hungary and Austria. Germany took in nearly a million; "Wir schaffen das," said Angela Merkel.

sites.text: Half a million people landed on the island in 2015.
